source.title: Compression via Pre-trained Transformers: A Study on Byte-Level Multimodal Data
source.authors: David Heurtel-Depeiges; Anian Ruoss; J. Veness; Tim Genewein

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure labels and surrounding text are garbled by web extraction, but the relevant scaling results are also described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study conducts model- and dataset-size sweeps and reports adjusted compression ratios, a different measure from held-out cross-entropy loss, to examine scaling-like behavior. It does not reproduce the original loss-law fitting procedure.
record.gate_note: The study minimizes sequential log-loss during training, but its scaling results report adjusted compression ratios on OOD data, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss. It does not fit loss exponents or test small-run extrapolation. The referenced findings from Kaplan et al. and Delétang et al. are not study results and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper runs model-size × dataset-size and model-size × context-size sweeps. It reports only adjusted compression ratio (compressed OOD data plus float16 model size) read from figures. It fits no power law, exponent or extrapolation. Model sizes span only 412K–947K parameters, about 2.3x, not orders of magnitude. The authors call the trends only 'akin to' scaling laws. The measure folds in parameter cost and is evaluated out of distribution, so it cannot show the power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal split or exponent dependence any version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion, however, is that small pre-trained byte-level transformers beat standard compressors on OOD data even after counting parameters, with weak out-of-modality transfer. The scaling remarks are secondary and qualitative: compression improves with model and data size, OOD evaluation makes overfitting (for images) more likely, and the context/model trade-off is modality-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: This is a byte-level multimodal compression study of relatively small transformers, evaluated by adjusted compression ratio on OOD data; it does not fit the original language-model held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The context-size versus model-size trade-off differs by modality. Image-only training shows overfitting, while the tested multimodal mixture does not; multimodal results are slightly worse than unimodal results.

fits_no_version.finding: Adjusted OOD compression ratio (data plus model size) improves as model size (412K–947K) and dataset size (33–165GB) grow, for audio, text and image byte models (Fig. 4). Image-only models gradually overfit; a multimodal mixture prevents this but compresses slightly worse (Fig. A1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For small byte-level transformers, size-penalised OOD compression improves qualitatively with model and data scale but can overfit under distribution shift, depending on modality and data mixture.

fits_no_version.finding: The best split of compute between context length and model size depends on modality. For text, the best models use contexts of 2048 bytes or less; for images, 8192 bytes with smaller models; audio is complex (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal context-length/model-size trade-off for byte-level transformers is modality-dependent.

record.problems: Scaling outcomes are reported as adjusted compression ratios rather than held-out cross-entropy losses. Figure 4 and Figure 5 do not provide clearly extractable numerical values in the supplied text, and the reported scaling sweeps do not fit exponents or test extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible scaling findings were left out. Other compression-ratio results, including the compressor comparisons in Table A2 and the sliding-window and evaluation-size ablations, do not measure any of the named scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported or fitted against parameters, tokens or compute. The parameter range is under one order of magnitude.
No fixed-compute parameter/token optimum and no growth exponent with compute.
No fixed-parameter comparison of depth or width shape.
Image and audio byte models are trained, but no power-law form is fitted for any modality.
No exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across setups or fitting methods.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 link and limits_scope label are dropped. No fit exists, the measure includes model size and OOD shift, and the parameter range is tiny. 'Scaling-law-like' is only the authors' qualitative description. This is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
Although the study sweeps model and dataset sizes, it does not identify a fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter-count and token-count allocation or fit their growth with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates compression across text, image, and audio, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.

The study reports scaling-like adjusted-compression-ratio sweeps and image overfitting, but does not fit or compare exponents, test the effects of parameter-counting or fitting methods, or measure how compute-optimal parameter/token allocations vary with setup.

rows.subject: Unimodal transformer sweep (audio)
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and training dataset size, then evaluated adjusted compression ratio.
rows.value: figure only; the text describes improved compression as model and dataset size increase
rows.note: The text describes the scaling trends as akin to LLM scaling laws, while noting that OOD evaluation makes scaling more complex. Figure values are not transcribed clearly.
rows.check: Adjusted OOD compression ratio over a ~2.3x parameter range, with no fit. It cannot show a power law or exponent dependence, so it should not link to V7. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Unimodal transformer sweep (image)
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and training dataset size, then evaluated adjusted compression ratio.
rows.value: figure only; the text reports gradual overfitting on the image dataset
rows.note: The authors say OOD evaluation makes models more prone to overfitting, including the largest image models, so scaling is more complex than traditional LLM scaling laws.
rows.check: Same measure issue as r1. The image overfitting is a qualitative non-monotonic trend in an OOD, size-penalised metric. It is not evidence about fitted exponents or bending of a held-out loss law.

rows.subject: Unimodal transformer sweep (text)
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and training dataset size, then evaluated adjusted compression ratio.
rows.value: figure only; the text describes improved compression as model and dataset size increase
rows.note: The text describes scaling-like trends and says increasing model and dataset size boosts compression. Figure values are not transcribed clearly.
rows.check: Same as r1: qualitative improvement only, with no power-law fit, so the V7 link is not justified.

rows.subject: Multimodal transformer sweep
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and dataset size for a uniform multimodal training mixture.

conditions.value: 55GB each of audio, image, and text

rows.value: figure only; the text reports no overfitting, but slightly worse compression ratios than unimodal training
rows.note: The authors describe the multimodal mixture as regularizing the models, with no observed overfitting even for the largest tested image models.
rows.check: Multimodal sweep from Fig. A1. The comparison with unimodal training is about data mixture, not scaling-law form or fit choices. The text gives no numbers.

rows.subject: Unimodal transformer sweep (text)
rows.operation_detail: Swept context-window length and model size across training compute budgets.
rows.value: figure only; the text says the best text models use a context window of 2048 bytes or less, with larger models beneficial
rows.note: The authors state that the compute trade-off depends strongly on modality; shorter contexts are better for text.
rows.check: This is a context-length versus model-size compute trade-off, not a parameter versus token allocation. No optimum is fitted as a power of compute, so it does not bear on V3 or V7.

rows.subject: Unimodal transformer sweep (image)
rows.operation_detail: Swept context-window length and model size across training compute budgets.
rows.value: figure only; the text says the best overall compromise uses a context window of 8192 bytes, with a smaller model
rows.note: The context/model trade-off differs from text and is described as modality-dependent.
rows.check: Same as r5. It is a context/model trade-off for images, with no compute-optimal fit.

rows.subject: Unimodal transformer sweep (audio)
rows.operation_detail: Swept context-window length and model size across training compute budgets.
rows.value: figure only; the text describes a complex trade-off, with intermediate context length and larger models performing better overall
rows.note: The text says the direction reverses for short contexts, further indicating modality-dependent trade-offs.
rows.check: Same as r5. The audio trade-off is described only qualitatively.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Unimodal OOD sweeps and context/model-size sweeps across the tested modalities
reader_labels.reason: Scaling-like improvements are reported, but image overfitting and modality-dependent context/model trade-offs make the behavior more complex than a single general trend (r1-r3, r5-r7). The multimodal sweep avoids the reported overfitting but has slightly worse compression than unimodal training (r4).
